title: Manthara's trap
hookLine: an old debt of gratitude, and a maid who turns it into a trap
carry: matsarya: envy bends good things into weapons

cards: Years before Rama was born, the gods went to war with a demon named Shambara and asked King Dasharatha to fight beside them. Kaikeyi rode with him.

The king was badly wounded and fell unconscious, and Kaikeyi drove his chariot out of the fighting and saved his life. When he woke, he said: ask me for two things, anything. I'll ask later, she said.
And then, it seems, she forgot. Manthara didn't.

teach.h: THE KING OWES YOU TWO BOONS.
teach.b: Kaikeyi asks how to stop the coronation, and Manthara answers with Kaikeyi's own story. The king owes you two boons. Ask now.

First, that Bharata be consecrated as heir. Second, that Rama be sent to the Dandaka forest for fourteen years, living as an ascetic: long enough, Manthara reasons, for Bharata to win the people's hearts.
Then the plan: go to the anger room, where a wronged queen goes, and lie on the bare floor. Refuse his gifts. Make him swear first, and only then ask.

teach.h: A TRAP MADE OF GOOD THINGS.
teach.b: She builds the trap out of good things: the king's love, his pride in keeping his word, and Kaikeyi's own courage in battle. All of it is about to become a weapon.
Earlier that same day, she heard Rama would be heir and was glad; she saw no difference between Rama and her own son. What changed? Hindu teachers have a name for it.
They count six inner enemies, the shad-ripu: desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and matsarya, envy, the ache when someone else rises. Manthara never has to make Kaikeyi hate Rama.
She only has to keep her picturing Kausalya's son on the throne and her own son standing behind him.

teach.h: MATSARYA: ENVY BENDS GOOD THINGS INTO WEAPONS.
teach.b: Many teachers read this night as envy at work: it doesn't throw away your good things, it bends them toward someone you've stopped seeing clearly.
The first step against an inner enemy is to see it and call it by its name. Kaikeyi never does. Manthara's part is done.
The rest will be done by a promise.

how: The kopa-griha, or anger room, appears in this episode of the Ayodhya Kanda. Hindu teachers list six inner enemies, the shad-ripu: kama, krodha, lobha, moha, mada and matsarya (desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride and envy). Many families close their prayers with sarve bhavantu sukhinah, may all be happy.

o: Kausalya's servant, who warns the king of a plot
Kaikeyi's maid, who turns an old promise into a trap
the queen who saved Dasharatha's life in battle

games.q: the old promise — tap the pairs.
p: drove the wounded king to safety
envy, one of six inner enemies
where a wronged queen lies down

s: the boons were a wedding gift
they were the king's thanks for saving his life in battle.
Manthara tells Kaikeyi to refuse gifts and make the king swear first
that's the heart of her plan.
Manthara has to make Kaikeyi hate Rama
she only keeps her picturing Bharata standing behind Kausalya's son. envy does the rest.

games.q: you're Kaikeyi's oldest friend. she's on the anger room floor, sure Kausalya's son is about to take everything. by the teaching on inner enemies, what helps most?
o: agree with her; she deserves to come first.
help her name it as envy, and remind her how glad she was for Rama this morning.
tell her she should be ashamed of feeling that way.
games.why: matsarya is an enemy within, and the first step is seeing it for what it is. that morning Kaikeyi was glad for Rama; by night, envy had bent her love out of shape.

practice: Think of someone whose good news stung a little lately: a friend's win, a sibling's praise. Don't push the feeling away. Breathe in, and name it plainly: this is matsarya, envy.

Breathe out, and picture that person's face. Many Hindus end their prayers with sarve bhavantu sukhinah, may all be happy. If you pray, say it now with that person in mind, and ask God to bless them by name.
If you don't pray, simply wish them well, and mean one small part of it.

wordCard.voice: Manthara. The maid who turns an old promise into a trap; in many retellings, the very picture of a voice that feeds envy.

orig.note: Sanskrit mātsarya: envy, resentment at another's good; one of the six inner enemies (shad-ripu).

carryVoice: Your line: matsarya: envy bends good things into weapons. Tomorrow, the king walks in. Day five hundred nineteen, done.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda 9 (the Shambara war; the two boons; Manthara's plan; the anger room)
